composition: Binary Fe–Al alloy with a nominal content of 16 at.% Al; the real composition of the polycrystalline Fe-16 alloy is 16.0–16.1 at.% Al, corresponding to 8.4–8.5 wt.% Al. The base element is Fe (99.99% purity, further purified by zone melting to minimise impurities) and the alloying element is Al (99.999% purity); Al was added to produce solid-solution hardening, reduce density and provide oxidation and high-temperature corrosion resistance. Impurities were intentionally kept very low: carbon <20–40 wt.ppm and Si <20–80 wt.ppm, with other elements (Co, Ni, As) reported only as upper limits (<30–40 wt.ppm). Alloys in this study were kept below 100 wt.ppm C, in contrast to earlier Fe–Al studies that contained 300–600 wt.ppm C and whose ordering/embrittlement results could be complicated by that carbon.
summary: Polycrystalline as-cast binary Fe–16 at.% Al alloy (nominal; real 16.0–16.1 at.% / 8.4–8.5 wt.% Al) prepared by vacuum induction melting of high-purity Fe and Al and solidification in a Cu mould into rods of usually 18 mm diameter. It is one member of a series of binary Fe–Al alloys (4–18 at.% Al) used to clarify how strength and ductility depend on Al content and on atomic short-range ordering, tested in compression and tension at room temperature and at −100 °C. In the as-cast state the alloy is a single-phase, coarse-grained (~1 mm) bcc Fe–Al solid solution containing no second phases; it deforms ductilely at room temperature (UTS just below 500 MPa, elongation ~18%) but becomes brittle with a much smaller fracture strain at −100 °C.
